title: Governance & Compliance

techniques.name: India’s DPDP Act and Rules
techniques.q: What does Indian data-protection law require of my agent?
techniques.what: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and its Rules (notified 13 November 2025) govern personal data processed in India. An agent that reads KYC documents or chats with customers is processing personal data, so it needs an itemised notice, specific consent or another lawful basis, collection limited to the purpose, reasonable security safeguards, contracts with processors such as model vendors, breach reporting and erasure when the purpose ends, including from vector stores and agent memory.
use: Any agent that sees customers’ personal data
Before sending personal data to a model vendor
When designing memory, logs and retention
metrics: itemised, plain language, before or at collection
free, specific, informed; as easy to withdraw as to give
only the data the stated purpose needs
encryption, masking, access control, logs kept at least a year
inform the Board without delay; detailed report within 72 hours
delete when the purpose ends or consent is withdrawn
steps: Map every place personal data flows: prompts, retrieval, memory, logs, vendors
Write purpose-specific notices and consent, and record them
Mask or tokenise identifiers before they reach the model or logs
Build breach and erasure runbooks that reach every store
pitfalls: Deleting from the main database but not from embeddings, memory or caches
Sending raw Aadhaar or PAN details to an offshore model with no processor contract
Treating 13 May 2027 as far away: the data flows are being designed now
tools: Microsoft Presidio for PII detection and masking
Consent-management platforms, and registered consent managers from November 2026
Data-flow inventories in your GRC tool
Vault or cloud KMS for tokenisation keys
techniques.remember: Say why, ask specifically, take less, protect it, delete it, report breaches fast.
techniques.cap: Penalties are maximums set by the Act; dates as notified. Not legal advice.

techniques.name: RBI and SEBI Expectations for AI
techniques.q: What will my financial regulator ask about our AI?
techniques.what: RBI’s FREE-AI framework (August 2025) sets seven sutras and recommendations for banks and NBFCs: a board-approved AI policy, an AI inventory, audits, customer disclosure and grievance routes, and incident reporting. RBI’s draft model risk guidance (June 2026) extends model governance to AI, including third-party models, kill switches and human oversight. SEBI’s Regulation 16C (February 2025) makes intermediaries solely responsible for AI output, data and compliance, and SEBI has announced guidelines with kill switches and human-in-the-loop controls.
use: Banks, NBFCs, brokers and other regulated entities using AI
Before a customer-facing AI launch
When a vendor supplies the model
metrics: board-approved, covering the AI life cycle
every AI use, tiered by risk
you own outputs, including a vendor’s
independent testing before and after launch
human in the loop for high-impact decisions; kill switch
disclosure, a human option, grievance redress
steps: List every AI use and tier it by customer impact
Adopt a board-approved AI policy with named owners
Validate each model, including vendor models, before launch
Add kill switches, human review for high-impact decisions and customer disclosure
pitfalls: Assuming the vendor is responsible for the vendor’s model
Treating a customer-facing agent like an internal tool
Waiting for final SEBI guidelines before building basic controls
tools: A GRC platform for the AI inventory
Ticketing for grievance and incident routes
techniques.remember: Inventory it, own it, test it, stop it, tell the customer.
techniques.cap: Status as of 26 Sep 2026: RBI MRM guidance is a draft; SEBI guidelines are announced, not final.

techniques.name: EU AI Act Risk Tiers
techniques.q: Does the EU AI Act apply to us, and at what tier?
techniques.what: The EU AI Act classifies AI systems by risk. A few practices are prohibited; high-risk systems, including creditworthiness scoring of individuals and life and health insurance pricing, need risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight and conformity assessment; chatbots and generated content carry transparency duties; everything else is minimal risk. It reaches Indian firms whose systems are used in the EU or whose outputs are used there. The 2026 Digital Omnibus moved Annex III high-risk duties to 2 December 2027.
use: Serving EU residents or EU clients
Credit, insurance or hiring decisions
Global banks and brokers with EU operations
metrics: since 2 Feb 2025; fines up to €35m or 7% of turnover
from 2 Dec 2027; fines up to €15m or 3%
from 2 Aug 2026: say it is AI, label synthetic content
no new duties beyond AI literacy
builds or places it on the market: most duties
uses it: oversight, logs, informing people
steps: Check territorial scope: are EU residents affected?
Classify each use case by tier
Work out whether you are provider or deployer
Map the duties and dates, and plan backwards from them
pitfalls: Assuming non-EU firms are exempt
Treating fraud detection as credit scoring: it is carved out
Missing the chatbot transparency duty that already applies
tools: EU AI Act Service Desk and compliance checker
Harmonised standards from CEN-CENELEC JTC 21 (in progress)
techniques.remember: Scope first, then tier, then role, then dates.
techniques.cap: Dates reflect Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus), in force 27 July 2026. Not legal advice.

techniques.name: NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001
techniques.q: How do we run AI governance as a system, not a scramble?
techniques.what: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organises AI risk work into Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, with a Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) for LLM-specific risks. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is a certifiable AI management system standard: policy, risk and impact assessment, controls, competence, operation, internal audit and management review. Neither is Indian law, but both give a structure that makes RBI, SEBI, DPDP and EU evidence repeatable, and one well-built control usually satisfies several frameworks.
use: Building a governance programme from scratch
Clients or partners asking for certification
Mapping one set of controls to several regulations
metrics: prioritise and treat risks, respond to incidents
certifiable; Annex A lists AI controls
guidance on AI system impact assessment
steps: Adopt one framework as the backbone
Build a control library, each control mapped to every framework it serves
Run impact assessments per use case
Audit internally and review with management on a schedule
pitfalls: Running separate compliance projects per regulation
Certifying the paperwork while systems drift
Frameworks without evals, red teaming and monitoring behind them
tools: NIST AI RMF Playbook and Generative AI Profile
Evaluation eval suites and Agent Security red teaming as evidence
techniques.remember: One control library, mapped many ways, audited on a schedule.
techniques.cap: Illustrative crosswalk; confirm mappings against the standards’ texts.

cmp.needs: An owner and a control library

techniques.name: Audit Trails and Explainability
techniques.q: Can we show exactly why the agent decided what it did?
techniques.what: An audit trail records, for every decision, what the agent saw, which model and prompt versions ran, which rules and documents it used, which tools it called, what it decided with reason codes, and who reviewed or overrode it. Records go to append-only storage with hash chaining or write-once retention so tampering is detectable, with personal data masked or tokenised, and kept for the legal retention period. Explainability for agents means reason codes and a replayable trace, not just a feature-importance chart.
use: Any decision a customer or regulator can challenge
KYC, credit, claims and complaints
Investigating incidents
steps: Define the questions an auditor will ask about a decision
Log the fields that answer each question, with versions
Write to append-only, hash-chained or write-once storage
Mask personal data and set retention to the legal period
pitfalls: Logging only the final answer
Logs editable by the team being audited
Raw Aadhaar or PAN numbers in logs
tools: Object storage with write-once retention (S3 Object Lock or equivalent)
SHAP or reason codes for scored models
techniques.remember: Every decision replayable, every record tamper-evident, no raw personal data.
techniques.cap: Retention periods vary by rule; KYC records are commonly kept five years after the relationship ends.

techniques.name: Model and System Cards
techniques.q: How do we document what the system is and where it fails?
techniques.what: A model card documents a model’s intended use, training data, evaluation results by subgroup and limitations. A system card does the same for the whole deployed agent: purpose and out-of-scope uses, data and legal basis, results overall and by segment, known failure modes, human oversight and kill switch, versions and a grievance contact. Different audiences get different versions: a full card for auditors and a plain one-page notice for customers.
use: Before launch and at every material change
Regulator inspections and client due diligence
Customer-facing AI disclosures
steps: Draft the card from the eval suite and the inventory, not from memory
Break results down by segment: language, region, document type
State limitations plainly, with mitigations
Version the card with the system and publish a customer summary
pitfalls: Reporting only an overall average
Cards written once at launch and never updated
A customer notice written in legal language
tools: Your eval reports (Evaluation) as the source
techniques.remember: What it is for, how well it works, for whom it fails, who to call.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: 94% overall hides 71% on scanned regional-language documents.

techniques.name: Third-Party and Vendor Model Risk
techniques.q: What happens to us when our model provider changes, leaks or goes down?
techniques.what: When a bank or broker runs its agent on someone else’s model, the provider’s terms, versions and outages become the firm’s own risk, and regulators still hold the firm accountable. Vendor model risk management covers due diligence before signing (training use, retention and zero data retention, data residency, SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001 and 42001), contracts with SLAs, audit rights and incident notice, pinned model versions with evals on every change, concentration risk with a tested fallback and an exit plan, and ongoing monitoring. The regulatory duties themselves sit in the DPDP and RBI and SEBI techniques; this one is the vendor-facing engineering and contracting that meets them.
use: Before signing with an LLM provider or AI vendor
Any regulated workload that runs on a third-party model
When a provider announces a deprecation or changes its terms
metrics: training use, retention days, zero data retention, region
SOC 2 Type II, ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 42001 reports and their scope
SLA, audit and regulator access, incident notice, sub-processors
pinned dated model; evals re-run before any change
second provider behind one interface, failover drilled
documented plan, data return and deletion, time to migrate
steps: Run due diligence on data terms, residency and certificates before any customer data flows
Write the contract: SLA, audit and regulator access, incident notice, sub-processors, exit
Pin model versions and re-run the eval suite on every version or deprecation change
Keep a tested fallback behind an abstraction layer, a written exit plan, and review the vendor on a schedule
pitfalls: Calling a floating alias, so the provider changes behaviour in production without a release
A fallback provider that has never carried real traffic, or has weaker data terms than the primary
Relying on a certificate without reading its scope, or on a vendor’s word instead of the contract
tools: Provider data-control and zero data retention settings
LiteLLM or a similar gateway for pinned routing and fallbacks
promptfoo or your own regression evals
A third-party risk module in your GRC tool
techniques.remember: Read the terms, pin the version, test the fallback, write the exit, keep watching.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Godavari Bank, a fictional private bank, 2,00,000 complaint conversations a month on one overseas provider. Educational, not legal advice.

cmp.scope: Every external model or AI vendor
cmp.needs: Contract terms, pinned versions and a tested fallback
cmp.best: Silent changes and a single point of failure

techniques.name: AI Incident Management and Reporting
techniques.q: When an AI system causes harm, who decides, who is told, and by when?
techniques.what: Operational incident response restores service; AI incident management is the governance around it. It defines what counts as an AI incident (unfair decisions, harmful or false outputs, privacy leaks, unsafe actions, security compromise, not just outages), sets a severity scale, keeps a register with owners and evidence, and runs notification playbooks with the clocks that may apply: for example CERT-In’s 6-hour reporting of cyber incidents, DPDP breach intimation to the Data Protection Board and affected people, sector regulators such as RBI, SEBI or IRDAI, and serious-incident reporting under the EU AI Act for high-risk systems. Each incident ends with a root cause, corrective actions and a report to the board or risk committee, and the register feeds risk reviews. This is an educational summary, not legal advice; confirm current obligations with counsel. On-call response and trace replay are covered by Incident Response in module 11.
use: Regulated firms using AI in credit, claims, trading or customer service
Any AI system that makes or shapes decisions about people
Organisations adopting ISO/IEC 42001 or the NIST AI RMF
metrics: harm types that count: unfair outcomes, false or harmful outputs, privacy, unsafe actions, security
S1–S4 by people affected, harm, reversibility and regulatory exposure
one record per incident: owner, evidence, timeline, decisions, status
CERT-In 6 hours for cyber incidents; DPDP breach intimation; sector regulators; EU AI Act for high-risk systems
cause, corrective and preventive actions, verified before closure
repeat-incident rate and themes reported to the risk committee
steps: Write a definition and severity matrix, agreed with risk, legal and compliance
Keep one register with owners, evidence and a timeline for every incident
Build notification playbooks with clocks and pre-approved templates per regulator
Close with root cause and verified corrective actions; review themes quarterly
pitfalls: Treating a biased model as “working fine” because nothing crashed
Discovering the notification clock after it has run out
Closing incidents on a fix that was never verified, so they recur
tools: An incident register (Jira, ServiceNow or a GRC tool)
techniques.remember: Define it, grade it, log it, notify on the clock, fix the cause.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Arogya Kosh, a fictional health insurer, uses AI for claims triage and a customer chatbot.

cmp.scope: Harm from AI systems, not just outages

techniques.name: Content Provenance and Synthetic-Media Labelling
techniques.q: Can people tell that an image, video or voice was made by AI?
techniques.what: Generative tools that produce realistic images, video or voice increasingly have to mark their output. Three layers work together: a visible label or audio disclosure people notice, signed provenance metadata such as C2PA Content Credentials that records how the file was made, and an invisible watermark that can survive screenshots and re-encoding when metadata is stripped. In India, the IT Amendment Rules 2026 (notified 16 February, in force 20 February 2026) require intermediaries offering tools that create synthetically generated audio-visual content to label it prominently, embed permanent metadata or an identifier where feasible and not allow labels or metadata to be removed, with extra user-declaration duties for significant social media intermediaries. The EU AI Act adds transparency duties for synthetic content and deepfakes from August 2026. This is an educational summary, not legal advice; confirm scope and details with counsel.
use: Tools that generate realistic images, video, voice or avatars
Marketing and media teams publishing AI-made assets
Platforms that host user uploads and must detect and label synthetic media
metrics: text or icon on images and video; spoken disclosure at the start of audio
signed manifest: tool, time, edits; verifiable, but often stripped on upload
invisible signal in pixels or audio; survives many edits; needs a detector
share of assets still identifiable after sharing, cropping and re-encoding
users cannot remove labels or metadata inside your tool
audio-visual content that looks real; text-only and routine edits are treated differently
steps: Map which outputs are realistic synthetic media and where they are published
Add visible labels and audio disclosures by default, not as a user option
Sign C2PA manifests and add an invisible watermark; stop users removing them
Test survival after real sharing paths, and keep records for audits
pitfalls: Relying on metadata alone, which most sharing paths strip
A label the user can switch off in the export dialog
Labelling text chat output under rules meant for audio-visual deepfakes, while missing the voice clones
tools: Pillow or FFmpeg for visible labels
techniques.remember: Label it, sign it, watermark it, and don’t let anyone strip it.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Rangmanch Studio, a fictional ad-tech company, generates images and Hindi voice ads for Indian brands.

AADHAAR = re.compile(r"\b\d{4}\s?\d{4}\s?(\d{4})\b")

def record_consent(customer_id, purpose, notice_version, lang):     #@1
    return consent_store.insert({"customer_id": customer_id,         #@2
        "purpose": purpose, "notice_version": notice_version,        #@2
        "language": lang, "given_at": now(), "withdrawn_at": None})  #@2

def mask(text):                                                     #@3
    return AADHAAR.sub(lambda m: "XXXX XXXX " + m.group(1), text)    #@3

def ask_model(customer_id, purpose, text):
    if not consent_store.active(customer_id, purpose):               #@2
        raise PermissionError(f"no active consent for {purpose}")
    return vendor_llm.complete(mask(text))    # processor contract   #@4

def on_breach(incident):                                            #@5
    board.notify(incident.summary, when="without delay")             #@5
    schedule(board.full_report, within_hours=72)                     #@5
    notify_affected_customers(incident)                              #@5

STORES = [primary_db, vector_store, agent_memory, cache, log_archive]  #@6
def erase(customer_id):                                             #@6
    return {s.name: s.delete_customer(customer_id) for s in STORES}  #@6
steps: An itemised notice first

Before collecting anything, tell the customer what data, for which purpose, and how to withdraw or complain, in plain English or a language they choose. The notice version is recorded with the consent.
Consent per purpose
KYC and marketing are separate purposes with separate records. The agent checks for active consent for this purpose before any processing.
Take less: mask identifiers
The model does not need a full Aadhaar number to check an address. Masking to the last four digits before the call keeps it out of prompts, vendor systems and logs.
Bind the vendor
A model vendor processing personal data for you is a data processor. A contract binds it to your purpose and safeguards; you remain responsible.
Breach: fast, then in full
Inform the Data Protection Board and affected people without delay, and give the Board a detailed report within 72 hours. A runbook makes that possible at 2 a.m.
Erase every copy
Erasure must reach the vector store, agent memory, caches and logs, not only the main database. Nivesh Credit’s first test reached 2 of 5 stores.

steps: Scope first
The Act reaches providers and deployers outside the EU when the system’s output is used in the EU. The fintech’s scoring of students in Germany is in scope; its Indian-only book is not.
A few practices are banned
Manipulation, exploiting vulnerabilities, social scoring and emotion recognition at work have been prohibited since 2 February 2025.
High-risk: Annex III
Creditworthiness scoring of individuals and life and health insurance pricing are high-risk. Fraud detection is carved out of the credit category.
Your role sets your duties
A provider builds the system and carries the heaviest duties; a deployer uses it and must keep logs, oversee it and inform people.
Dates after the Omnibus
Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026, moved Annex III high-risk duties to 2 December 2027. Plan backwards from that date.
Chatbots: say it is AI
Transparency duties apply from 2 August 2026: people must know they are dealing with AI, and synthetic content must be labelled.

steps: Pick a backbone
NIST AI RMF for risk practice, ISO/IEC 42001 when clients want a certificate. Many banks use both.
One control, many mappings
Each control lists every framework and clause it serves. An AI policy counts for NIST Govern, ISO 5.2, RBI’s policy recommendation and the EU quality system.
Map: assess impact per use case
An impact assessment for each AI use is NIST’s Map function and ISO 42001’s AI system impact assessment; ISO/IEC 42005 gives guidance.
Measure and Manage need engineering
Eval suites, red teaming, monitoring and incident runbooks from the Evaluation, AgentOps and Agent Security modules are the evidence behind these functions.
Measure coverage per framework
Coverage shows where one library falls short for a given regulator, instead of starting a new project.
Audit and review on a schedule
Internal audit and management review keep the system alive. The bank cut evidence requests from 400 items to 150.

def record(self, case_id, doc_bytes, fields, run, decision, reasons, reviewer):
    entry = {
        "case_id": case_id, "ts": now(),                                 #@6
        "input_sha256": sha256(doc_bytes),                               #@1
        "fields": mask_pii(fields),          # no raw Aadhaar or PAN     #@5
        "model": run.model, "prompt_version": run.prompt_version,        #@2
        "policy_clauses": run.clauses_used,                              #@3
        "tool_calls": run.tool_calls,                                    #@3
        "decision": decision, "reason_codes": reasons,                   #@3
        "reviewer": reviewer,                                            #@3
        "prev": self.prev}                                               #@4
    entry["hash"] = _hash(entry)                                         #@4
    self.store.append(entry)                 # write-once bucket         #@4
    self.prev = entry["hash"]

def verify(entries):                                                     #@4
    return all(e["prev"] == p["hash"] for p, e in zip(entries, entries[1:]))  #@4
# retention: longest legal period that applies                           #@6
steps: What did it see?
A hash of the uploaded document proves which file was read without storing it twice; the extracted fields show what the agent took from it.
Which system was it?
Model and prompt versions. Without them, a replay cannot tell whether a later change caused the decision.
Why, and who?
The policy clauses used, the tool calls and results, reason codes, and the reviewer. The disputed rejection turned out to be an address mismatch under a named clause.
Make edits detectable
Each record carries the previous record’s hash and goes to write-once storage. Changing or deleting any record breaks the chain.
No raw personal data
Mask identifiers in the log. The audit trail must not become the biggest store of Aadhaar numbers in the company.
Keep it long enough
Timestamps, and retention set to the longest legal requirement; KYC records are commonly kept five years after the relationship ends.

steps: Due diligence before data flows

Godavari Bank, a fictional private bank, checks four things before any complaint text reaches the provider: no training on its data, retention it has agreed (zero data retention here, instead of the default 30 days of logs), processing in India, and current SOC 2 Type II and ISO/IEC 27001 reports whose scope covers the API it will use.
A contract you can enforce

The contract turns assurances into obligations: a 99.9% availability SLA, notice of incidents within 6 hours so the bank can meet its own CERT-In and DPDP clocks, audit and access rights for the bank and its regulator, notice before new sub-processors, and an exit clause for data return and deletion.
Pin a dated version
The code names a dated snapshot, not a floating alias. With an alias the provider can change the model behind the same name, and the bank’s complaint summaries change with no release on its side.
Evals on every change

A deprecation notice or a new snapshot triggers the eval suite: 400 labelled complaints. If the score drops more than 2 points below the baseline, the change is blocked and the pin stays. Otherwise the new version is proposed through the normal release review.
A tested fallback

All calls go through one function. If the primary provider is down or times out, the same request goes to a second provider on its own pinned version, with the same data terms. A fallback counts only if it has carried real traffic in a drill.
Keep watching, and plan the exit

Each month someone checks deprecation notices, terms changes, SLA reports and certificate expiry, and drills the failover. Once a year the exit plan is rehearsed: which prompts move, which evals prove the new model, how data comes back and is deleted, and how long it takes.

SEVERITY = {                     # agreed with risk, legal, compliance  #@1
  "S1": "many people harmed, or irreversible, or regulator-reportable",
  "S2": "a group harmed and reversible; possible regulatory exposure",
  "S3": "individuals affected, quickly reversible",
  "S4": "near miss, no one harmed"}

def open_incident(signal):
    inc = register.create(title=signal.title, system=signal.system,       #@2
                          owner=on_call_risk_owner(), evidence=signal.traces)
    inc.harm = classify_harm(signal)       # unfair, false, privacy, unsafe, security  #@1
    inc.severity = grade(inc, SEVERITY)                                   #@2
    for clock in playbook.clocks_for(inc):    # CERT-In, DPDP, IRDAI, EU AI Act  #@3
        schedule(clock.deadline(inc.detected_at), clock.template, approver="CCO")
    return inc

def close_incident(inc):
    assert inc.root_cause and inc.capa                                     #@4
    assert verify_fix(inc.capa, eval_set=inc.regression_cases)             #@4
    register.close(inc)
    risk_committee.add_to_quarterly(inc)                                   #@5

steps: Define what counts

Arogya Kosh, a fictional health insurer, agrees with risk, legal and compliance which harms count as AI incidents and how to grade them from S1 to S4. Unfair outcomes and privacy leaks count, not just outages.
Register and grade
Every signal that may be an AI incident opens a register entry with an owner, the traces as evidence and a severity.
Start the clocks

The playbook lists which notifications may apply, with deadlines from the detection time and pre-approved templates. A privacy leak starts the DPDP breach steps; a cyber attack the CERT-In 6-hour report; claims decisions may need a note to IRDAI.
Fix the cause, then close
An incident closes only with a root cause and corrective actions whose fix passes the regression cases added for it.
Report and learn
Closed incidents go to the quarterly risk committee pack with themes and repeat rates.
Two real-looking cases
A claims triage model rejected 1,240 valid claims from one region (S2, decisions reversed); the chatbot showed 38 customers another person’s policy number (S2, DPDP breach steps).

def system_card(system, evals, min_ok=0.85):
    overall = evals.accuracy()
    by_segment = evals.accuracy_by(["language", "doc_type", "region"])
    weak = {seg: acc for seg, acc in by_segment.items() if acc < min_ok}
    return {
        "name": system.name, "version": system.version,
        "intended_use": system.intended_use,
        "out_of_scope": system.out_of_scope,
        "data": {"sources": system.data_sources, "legal_basis": system.legal_basis},
        "results": {"overall": overall, "by_segment": by_segment},
        "limitations": system.known_limitations + [
            f"Below {min_ok:.0%} on {seg} ({acc:.0%}); routed to human review"
            for seg, acc in weak.items()],
        "oversight": {"human_review": system.review_rule, "kill_switch": system.flag},
        "change_log": system.changes,

    }

dpdp.title: Handling an erasure request
dpdp.explain: Only the primary database is cleared. The customer’s data stays in the vector store, the agent’s memory, caches and logs, so the response says “erased” when most copies remain.
dpdp.fix: results = {s.name: s.delete_customer(customer_id) for s in STORES}   # every store

also.3: Correct: recording that an erasure happened, without the personal data, is good practice.

finreg.title: The kill switch
finreg.explain: The default is True, so if the flag is missing or the flag service is down, the agent keeps running. A kill switch must fail closed: when in doubt, hand the request to people.

also.4: Correct: switching off should route work to humans, not drop it.

euai.title: Checking territorial scope
euai.explain: The EU AI Act reaches providers and deployers outside the EU when the system’s output is used in the EU. An Indian company scoring EU residents is in scope, but this check says it never is.

also.4: Correct once the condition is fixed.

frameworks.title: Measuring NIST coverage
frameworks.explain: It counts controls rather than functions covered, so four Measure controls report 100% while Govern, Map and Manage have nothing. Coverage must be the share of distinct functions met.
frameworks.fix: return len({f for h in hits for f in h} & functions) / len(functions)

also.2: Correct: the four NIST AI RMF functions.

audit.title: Verifying the decision log
audit.explain: Each record’s own hash is checked, but not its link to the previous record. Deleting a whole record, or rewriting one and its hash, goes undetected, so the chain gives no protection.
audit.fix: if _hash(body) != e["hash"] or e["prev"] != prev_hash: return False   # then prev_hash = e["hash"]

also.3: Correct: the hash covers every field except itself.

cards.title: Writing the limitations section
cards.explain: Only the overall figure is checked. At 94% it passes, so the card lists no limitations, although scanned regional-language documents score 71%. Check each segment.
cards.fix: weak = {s: a for s, a in evals.accuracy_by(["language", "doc_type"]).items() if a < min_ok}

also.2: Correct as a headline number, but not enough on its own.

vendor.title: A pinned version nobody uses
vendor.explain: The team pins a dated snapshot and gates changes on evals, but the call itself uses the floating alias. The provider can move model-a-latest to a new snapshot at any time, so behaviour changes in production and the eval gate never runs.

also.8: Correct: every candidate snapshot runs the same eval suite as the baseline.
also.9: Correct: a drop of more than 2 points blocks the change; smaller changes go to review.

dpdp.q: Walk me through what the DPDP Act and Rules mean for an agent that reads customers’ KYC documents.
dpdp.model: The agent processes personal data, so each purpose needs an itemised notice and specific consent or another lawful basis. Collect only what the purpose needs and mask identifiers such as Aadhaar before they reach prompts, vendors or logs. A model vendor is a processor, bound by a contract, while the firm stays responsible. Breaches go to the Data Protection Board without delay with a detailed report within 72 hours, and erasure must reach every store, including embeddings and memory.

dpdp.q: Why is erasure harder for an AI agent than for a normal application?
dpdp.model: Agents copy data into places a normal app does not: vector stores, long-term memory, conversation caches, traces and logs. Erasure has to fan out to every store and confirm each one, while respecting records that must be retained under other laws such as KYC rules, which should be restricted rather than kept in general use.

dpdp.q: When do DPDP obligations actually apply?
dpdp.model: The Rules were notified on 13 November 2025. Provisions setting up the Data Protection Board applied immediately, consent managers follow after 12 months in November 2026, and most substantive obligations, including notice, safeguards, breach reporting and erasure, apply after 18 months, from 13 May 2027.

finreg.q: A broker wants to launch a customer-facing agent on a vendor’s LLM. What will SEBI expect?
finreg.model: Regulation 16C makes the broker solely responsible for the tool’s output, for investor data and for compliance, so the vendor’s model must be validated and contracted with audit rights. SEBI has announced guidelines with kill switches and human-in-the-loop controls, so add a kill switch that fails closed, human review for high-impact actions, customer disclosure and incident reporting, and record it all in an AI inventory.

finreg.q: What does RBI’s FREE-AI framework recommend for banks?
finreg.model: FREE-AI, from August 2025, sets seven sutras, including public trust, the right to override, fairness, understandability and accountability regardless of autonomy, with recommendations under six pillars. For a bank that means a board-approved AI policy, an AI inventory by risk, independent audits, customer disclosure and grievance routes, and incident reporting. RBI’s June 2026 draft model risk guidance extends validation, kill switches and human oversight to AI and third-party models.

finreg.q: How do you keep AI controls proportionate?
finreg.model: Tier every AI use by its impact on customers. An internal tool needs an owner, validation and vendor terms; a customer-facing agent adds disclosure, grievance, incident reporting and a kill switch; an agent that decides about customers adds human review. That avoids both overloading internal tools and under-controlling customer-facing ones.

euai.q: Does the EU AI Act apply to an Indian fintech?
euai.model: It can, system by system. The Act applies to providers and deployers outside the EU when the output of their AI system is used in the EU. A credit model that scores EU residents is in scope, and as the builder the fintech is its provider; a model used only for Indian customers is not.

euai.q: Explain the EU AI Act’s risk tiers with financial examples.
euai.model: Prohibited practices, such as exploiting vulnerabilities to push products, are banned. High-risk systems include creditworthiness scoring of individuals and life and health insurance pricing, with duties on risk management, data governance, logging and human oversight. Chatbots carry transparency duties to tell people they are dealing with AI. Most other tools, including fraud detection, are minimal risk.

euai.q: What did the 2026 Digital Omnibus change?
euai.model: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force from 27 July 2026, moved Annex III high-risk obligations such as credit scoring to 2 December 2027 and product-embedded systems to 2 August 2028. Prohibitions have applied since February 2025, and transparency duties still apply from 2 August 2026, with a grace period to December 2026 for watermarking existing systems.

frameworks.q: NIST AI RMF or ISO/IEC 42001: which would you choose?
frameworks.model: They answer different needs. NIST AI RMF is a voluntary framework organised into Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, with a Generative AI Profile, and is excellent for risk practice. ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable management system that clients can verify. Many organisations use NIST to shape their risk practice and ISO 42001 as the management system they certify, with one control library behind both.

frameworks.q: How do you avoid running a separate compliance project for every regulation?
frameworks.model: Build one control library and map each control to every framework and regulation it satisfies. An eval report, an incident runbook or an AI policy is produced once and cited many times, and coverage per framework shows where new controls are needed rather than starting a new project.

frameworks.q: What engineering work sits behind an AI governance framework?
frameworks.model: Measure and Manage depend on engineering: pre-release eval suites, red teaming, production monitoring and incident runbooks. Without them, policies and certificates describe controls that do not exist. These come from the evaluation, AgentOps and security practices in earlier modules.

audit.q: Design an audit record for an AI agent that approves or rejects KYC applications.
audit.model: Each decision record holds a hash of the document and the extracted fields with identifiers masked, the model and prompt versions, the policy clauses and documents used, tool calls and results, the decision and reason codes, the human reviewer and any override, and timestamps. Records are hash-chained and written to append-only or write-once storage, and kept for the legal retention period.

audit.q: How do you explain an LLM agent’s decision to a regulator?
audit.model: Make the agent produce structured reason codes tied to written policy clauses, and log the evidence behind each code. Keep a replayable trace with model and prompt versions so the decision can be re-run. A free-text justification written by the model is not enough on its own.

audit.q: How can an audit log itself become a compliance risk?
audit.model: If it stores raw identifiers, the log becomes one of the largest stores of personal data, with the same DPDP duties. Mask or tokenise identifiers, restrict and log access to the log, and keep records for the legal retention period and no longer.

cards.q: What goes into a system card for a customer-facing agent?
cards.model: Intended use and out-of-scope uses, data sources and legal basis, results overall and by segment, known limitations with mitigations, human oversight and the kill switch, versions and a change log, and a grievance contact. Customers get a one-page plain summary; auditors get the full card.

cards.q: Why can averages give a false picture in model documentation?
cards.model: An overall figure is dominated by the largest groups, so a small segment can fail badly without moving it much. A KYC agent at 94% overall can be 71% on scanned regional-language documents, which are 10% of volume. Reporting results by segment is what exposes it.

cards.q: How do you keep documentation in step with a system that changes monthly?
cards.model: Generate the card from the same eval results used for release decisions, as part of the release pipeline, so each material change produces a new versioned card with its change log. Cards written by hand at launch go stale within a release or two.

vendor.q: Your bank wants to send customer complaint text to an overseas LLM provider. What would you check and agree before it goes live?
vendor.model: Check whether inputs are used for training, how long logs are kept and whether zero data retention is available, where the data is processed, which sub-processors are involved, and whether the SOC 2 Type II and ISO/IEC 27001 reports cover this service. Put the essentials into the contract: SLA, incident notice fast enough for the bank’s own CERT-In and DPDP clocks, audit and regulator access, sub-processor notice, and data return and deletion on exit. Under RBI’s outsourcing expectations and the DPDP Act the bank stays accountable, so the vendor is managed as a processor and an outsourced service, not trusted on its word.

vendor.q: A 99.9% monthly SLA sounds safe. Two independent providers each offer 99.9%. Roughly how much downtime a month does each allow, and what does a tested fallback change? Show the working.
vendor.model: A 30-day month has 43,200 minutes; 0.1% of that is 43.2 minutes each. If failures were independent, both providers would be down together only 0.1% × 0.1% of the time, about 2.6 seconds a month, so a working fallback turns an outage into a short failover. That only holds if the fallback has carried traffic in drills, is pinned and has the same data terms, and if the two providers do not share an upstream dependency.

vendor.q: Complaint summaries suddenly start dropping the amount in dispute, though nobody released anything. What happened and how do you stop it recurring?
vendor.model: The code most likely calls a floating alias and the provider moved it to a new snapshot, a silent behaviour change. Pin a dated snapshot, run the eval suite, including checks that amounts and dates survive, on any candidate before switching, and track the provider’s deprecation notices so migrations are planned, not forced.

aiincident.q: How would you set up AI incident management at a regulated firm?
aiincident.model: Agree a definition of AI incidents covering unfair, false, harmful, privacy, unsafe and security harms; a severity scale; a register with owners and evidence; notification playbooks with the deadlines that may apply and templates; and closure only with root cause and verified corrective action, reported to the risk committee. Confirm obligations with counsel.

aiincident.q: Detected Monday 10:30; report due in 72 hours. When?
The IT team says the chatbot privacy slip is not an incident because the service stayed up. Your reply?
aiincident.model: Incidents are about harm, not uptime. Showing someone else’s policy number may be a personal data breach, so open a register entry, grade it, involve legal and compliance to confirm DPDP breach steps and deadlines, and fix the cause.

provenance.q: How would you mark AI-generated media from your tool?
provenance.model: Label every realistic image and video visibly and start audio with a spoken disclosure, sign C2PA credentials, add an invisible watermark tied to an asset id, lock these in the tool, and test survival through real sharing apps.

provenance.q: Labels survive 70%; watermark survives 85% of the rest. Overall?
A client says C2PA metadata alone satisfies the new Indian rules. Your view?
provenance.model: The rules, in summary, also expect a prominent visible label or audio disclosure and that labels and metadata cannot be removed; metadata alone is also stripped by many apps. Add labels and a watermark, lock them, and confirm scope with counsel.

cases.title: The KYC agent the auditor is coming to see
cases.brief: Sahyog Securities uses an AI agent to verify KYC documents and approve or reject about 40,000 account applications a month, on a model from an overseas vendor. It has no clients or operations in the EU and generates no images, voice or video. A regulatory inspection is six weeks away, and the compliance head wants to know what to do first.
evidence: Decision logs hold only the outcome and a timestamp, in a database table the engineering team can edit.
Prompts send full Aadhaar and PAN numbers to the vendor's model hosted abroad. The contract has no data-processing or audit clauses.
There is no AI inventory and no board-approved AI policy. The agent rejects applications with no human review, and customers are not told AI is involved.
Applications with scanned regional-language documents are rejected about three times as often as average. Nobody has written this down or told anyone.
The vendor is called through a floating alias, and it has just announced a deprecation date for the snapshot currently in use.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.finreg: Start here, because symptom 3 is the set of things an inspector asks for in the first hour and the firm cannot produce any of them: no AI inventory, no board-approved policy, a customer-facing agent rejecting applications with no human review, and customers not told AI is involved. These are also the cheapest to produce in six weeks - an inventory, a policy, a human-review step on rejections, and a disclosure - and they frame everything else. Do not assume the vendor carries responsibility for the vendor's model, and do not wait for final guidelines before putting basic controls in.
why.audit: A decision a customer can challenge, logged as an outcome and a timestamp, in a table the engineering team can edit, is indefensible on two counts: it does not explain the decision and it is not evidence. Log the inputs, the retrieved documents, the model snapshot and the reasoning path - not just the answer - write to append-only storage the audited team cannot alter, and keep raw Aadhaar and PAN out of those logs.
why.dpdp: Full Aadhaar and PAN going to an offshore model with no data-processing or audit clauses is the named pitfall, and it is happening on every one of 40,000 monthly applications. Get the processor contract in place or stop sending the identifiers, minimise and tokenise what does go, and design erasure so it reaches embeddings, memory and caches rather than only the main database.
why.cards: Useful and achievable before the inspection: a system card describing what the agent does, what it is for, and where it fails - including the regional-language disparity broken out rather than hidden in an average - plus a customer notice in plain language rather than legal prose.
why.frameworks: Useful as the way to stop this recurring: one control set mapped to several obligations rather than a project per regulation. Six weeks is not long enough to certify anything, and certifying paperwork while the system drifts is the pitfall - but the mapping work pays from here on.
why.aiincident: Useful, and symptom 4 is one: regional-language documents rejected three times as often, never written down and never escalated, is a harm being treated as normal because nothing crashed. Decide now who owns such a finding, who must be told, and by when - before you discover the notification clock after it has run out.
why.vendor: Useful and newly urgent: a floating alias lets the vendor change behaviour in production with no release of yours, and a deprecation date has just been announced. Pin the snapshot, read the contract's audit and data terms, and make sure any fallback has carried real traffic and has terms no weaker than the primary.
why.euai: Not needed: the brief says no EU clients and no EU operations. Worth being deliberate about rather than assuming - Case 2 is a firm that assumed the same thing and was wrong.
why.provenance: Not needed: the agent reads documents and makes decisions, generating no images, video or synthetic voice. There is nothing to label.

firstWhy.audit: The deepest problem here and your second step - an editable outcome-only log is not evidence of anything. But an inspector opens with the inventory, the policy and whether a person reviews a rejection, and those take days rather than weeks. Produce the frame, then fill it with records that stand up.
firstWhy.dpdp: The largest ongoing legal exposure, repeating on all 40,000 applications a month, and it must be fixed. As the first move, though, the vendor contract is a negotiation on someone else's calendar, while the inventory, the policy and a human-review step on rejections are entirely within your control in the six weeks you actually have.
firstWhy.cards: Exactly what an inspector likes to be handed, and worth writing. But a card describes a system and its controls, and today there is no policy, no inventory and no human review to describe - you would be documenting the gap rather than closing it.

cases.model: Start with the financial-regulator expectations, because symptom 3 lists what an inspector asks for first and the firm has none of it: build the AI inventory, get a board-approved AI policy, put human review on rejections, and tell customers AI is involved - all achievable inside six weeks and all of which frame the rest. Then fix the audit trail: log inputs, retrieved documents, model snapshot and reasoning rather than an outcome and a timestamp, write to append-only storage the engineering team cannot edit, and keep raw Aadhaar and PAN out of the logs. Next address DPDP: either get a data-processing and audit contract with the overseas vendor or stop sending full identifiers, minimise and tokenise what does go, and design erasure to reach embeddings, memory and caches. Then write a system card documenting purpose and known failure modes - with the regional-language disparity broken out rather than buried in an average - and a plain-language customer notice. Adopt NIST AI RMF or ISO/IEC 42001 as the mapping layer so this is one control set rather than a project per regulator. Treat the regional-language disparity as a reportable incident with an owner and a clock, and pin the vendor snapshot now that a deprecation date exists. The EU AI Act does not apply, and nothing here generates synthetic media.
cases.note: Two techniques were ruled out by two facts in the brief - no EU exposure, no generated media - and Case 2 is a firm that believed the first of those and was wrong. Check the facts rather than the intuition.

finreg: Symptom 3 is a list rather than a single fault: no AI inventory, no board-approved policy, rejections with no human review, and customers not told AI is involved. An inspector arrives in six weeks. What are those four things, taken together?

They are the baseline a financial regulator expects of a regulated entity running customer-facing AI - and two of the pitfalls here concern who is responsible for a vendor's model and whether to wait for final guidance.
RBI and SEBI Expectations for AI. Read all three pitfalls: assuming the vendor is responsible, treating a customer-facing agent like an internal tool, and waiting for final guidelines.
audit: Symptom 1: the decision log holds an outcome and a timestamp, in a table the engineering team can edit. These are decisions customers can challenge. What two separate things are wrong?
One is about what is recorded - an answer is not a reason. The other is about who can change it afterwards, which decides whether it is evidence at all.
Audit Trails and Explainability. All three pitfalls are in this symptom and the next: logging only the final answer, logs editable by the audited team, and raw Aadhaar or PAN in logs.
dpdp: Symptom 2: full Aadhaar and PAN numbers going to a model hosted abroad, on a contract with no data-processing or audit clauses, across 40,000 applications a month. Which law is this, and which of its pitfalls is this exactly?
India's data-protection regime, and the specific failure is sending raw identifiers offshore with no processor contract. Think also about where else that data ends up, beyond the main database.
India's DPDP Act and Rules. Read the pitfall about raw Aadhaar or PAN sent offshore with no processor contract, and the one about deleting from the database but not from embeddings, memory or caches.

drop.euai: The EU AI Act applies at a tier depending on exposure and use. What does the brief say about this firm's EU clients and operations - and why is it worth checking rather than assuming?
drop.provenance: Content provenance labels images, video and synthetic voice so people can tell they were made by AI. What does this agent produce?

cases.firstHint: Your set is right. Now think about what six weeks actually buys: one of your choices is a negotiation with a vendor, one is an engineering rebuild, and one is a set of documents and a process change you fully control.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: An outcome-and-timestamp log in an editable table means no decision can be explained or evidenced at all.
Full Aadhaar and PAN go offshore on every application with no processor contract, which is the largest continuing legal exposure.
There is no inventory, no policy, no human review and no customer disclosure - the first things an inspector asks for, and the ones most achievable in six weeks.
whyFirst.why: Order by what the deadline allows and what frames the rest. The editable log is the deepest defect and the offshore identifiers the biggest ongoing exposure, and both are on the list - but the contract depends on the vendor's calendar and the logging is an engineering rebuild. An inventory, a board policy, human review on rejections and a customer notice are entirely yours to produce, they are what an inspection opens with, and everything else gets described against them.

cases.tag: The tier you did not check
cases.title: The credit agent that is high-risk under a law nobody read
cases.brief: An Indian-headquartered bank with a Dublin branch uses an agent to assess consumer loan applications from EU residents. The same platform also runs fraud detection and a customer-facing chatbot. The team believed that having a non-EU parent kept the EU AI Act out of scope, and built accordingly. It generates no images, video or synthetic voice.
evidence: The agent assesses creditworthiness for EU residents, which the EU AI Act places in its high-risk tier. The team assumed a non-EU parent made them exempt.
Fraud detection on the same platform is being held to the same high-risk controls, while the customer-facing chatbot discloses nothing about being AI.
There is no AI inventory, and three separate compliance projects run in parallel - one for DPDP, one for RBI, one for the EU - duplicating controls and contradicting each other.
Documentation is a launch-day model card reporting one overall accuracy figure, never updated since. The customer notice is written in legal language.
The fallback model provider has never carried real traffic and its data terms are weaker than the primary's.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.euai: Start here, because the premise the system was built on is wrong and everything inherits it. Serving EU residents brings you in scope regardless of where the parent sits - that is the first pitfall named - consumer creditworthiness is squarely high-risk, and two further errors follow from not having read the tiers: fraud detection is carved out and is being over-controlled at real cost, while the chatbot's transparency duty already applies and is being ignored. Establish the tier per use case before designing any control.
why.frameworks: Three parallel compliance projects duplicating and contradicting each other is the named pitfall, and it is why nothing is consistent. Adopt NIST AI RMF or ISO/IEC 42001 as one control set mapped to DPDP, the RBI expectations and the EU obligations at once - most controls serve all three, and the mapping is what turns three scrambles into one programme. Keep evals, red teaming and monitoring behind it, or you certify paperwork while the system drifts.
why.cards: High-risk classification brings documentation duties that a launch-day card with one accuracy number cannot meet. Report performance broken down rather than averaged - an overall figure is the named pitfall and it is exactly how a disparity in a credit model hides - update at every material change, and rewrite the customer notice in plain language, since a legal-prose notice does not discharge a transparency duty.
why.dpdp: Useful: Indian customers' data is in the same platform, and DPDP obligations run alongside the EU ones rather than instead of them. Largely covered by the mapped control set.
why.finreg: Useful: the RBI expectations apply to the bank as a regulated entity, including that the vendor's model is still the bank's responsibility. Also handled through the mapping rather than as its own project.
why.audit: Useful and required at this tier: a declined credit application is the textbook decision a customer can challenge, so inputs, features, model version and reasoning all need recording in storage the team cannot edit.
why.vendor: Useful and quietly dangerous: a fallback that has never carried real traffic will fail on the day it is needed, and one with weaker data terms turns a failover into a compliance breach. Test it with real traffic and align the terms.
why.aiincident: Useful: at high risk, a biased or failing credit model is reportable, so decide now who owns it, who must be told and by when - rather than finding the clock after it has expired.
why.provenance: Not needed: nothing here generates images, video or synthetic voice. The chatbot's disclosure duty is a transparency obligation under the Act, not a synthetic-media labelling one - which is a distinction worth keeping straight.

firstWhy.frameworks: The right way to stop three projects fighting each other, and your second step. But a control set is mapped against obligations, and the largest obligation here is currently misread in three different ways - in scope at all, fraud wrongly swept in, chatbot duty missed. Fix what you owe before organising how you deliver it.
firstWhy.cards: Genuinely required at this tier, and the single-accuracy-figure card is exactly how a credit model's disparity stays hidden. But what a card must contain depends on the tier, and the tier is precisely what nobody has established.
firstWhy.vendor: A real and underrated hole - an untested fallback with weaker data terms is a failover that becomes a breach. It is also one dependency, while the whole platform is built on a misreading of which law applies to it.

cases.model: Start with the EU AI Act risk tiers, because the system was built on a false premise that everything else inherits: serving EU residents brings you in scope whatever the parent's domicile, consumer creditworthiness assessment sits in the high-risk tier, fraud detection is carved out and is currently being over-controlled at real cost, and the chatbot's transparency duty already applies and is being ignored. Classify each use case properly first. Then adopt NIST AI RMF or ISO/IEC 42001 as a single control set mapped to the EU obligations, DPDP and the RBI expectations together, replacing three contradictory projects - with evals, red teaming and monitoring behind it rather than certification of paperwork. Then bring documentation up to what high risk requires: performance reported in segments rather than one overall accuracy figure, updated at every material change, and a customer notice in plain language instead of legal prose. Test the fallback provider with real traffic and align its data terms with the primary's, since an untested failover with weaker terms converts an outage into a breach. Build the audit trail a challengeable credit decision needs, and define incident ownership and notification timelines now. Nothing here generates synthetic media - the chatbot disclosure is a transparency duty, not a labelling one.
cases.note: Case 1 ruled the EU AI Act out on a fact; this firm ruled it out on an assumption and built a high-risk system around it. The same misreading then produced an opposite error - controls applied to fraud detection, which is carved out - so not knowing the tier costs money in both directions.

euai: Read symptoms 1 and 2 together. The team assumed a non-EU parent meant exemption while assessing creditworthiness for EU residents; fraud detection is being held to high-risk controls; and the chatbot discloses nothing. One body of law, three mistakes.
The question is which obligations attach to which use case, and at what level. Note that one of those three use cases is specifically carved out and another has a duty that already applies today.
EU AI Act Risk Tiers. All three pitfalls are in symptoms 1 and 2: assuming non-EU firms are exempt, treating fraud detection as credit scoring, and missing the chatbot transparency duty.
frameworks: Symptom 3: no AI inventory, and three separate compliance projects - DPDP, RBI, EU - running in parallel, duplicating controls and contradicting each other. What is the alternative to a project per regulation?
One set of controls, mapped to several obligations at once, run as a system. And a warning about what certification is worth if the operational practice is not behind it.
NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001. Read the pitfalls about separate compliance projects per regulation and about certifying paperwork while systems drift.
cards: Symptom 4: a launch-day model card with one overall accuracy figure, never updated, and a customer notice in legal language. For a credit model, what does a single overall figure hide?
Documentation of what the system is and where it fails - which means per-segment performance rather than an average, kept current, with the customer-facing part written to be understood.
Model and System Cards. All three pitfalls apply: reporting only an overall average, cards written once at launch, and a notice in legal language.

drop.provenance: Content provenance labels synthetic images, video and voice. What does this platform generate - and is the chatbot's disclosure duty a labelling rule or a transparency one?

cases.firstHint: Your set is right. Notice that one body of law has been misread three ways here - including once in the direction of spending too much - and ask what every control you design is measured against.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: Three parallel compliance projects are duplicating and contradicting each other, so the programme is structurally broken.
The whole system was built on the belief that a non-EU parent meant exemption, which is wrong and determines every obligation that follows.
A launch-day card with one accuracy figure cannot meet the documentation duties of a high-risk credit system.
whyFirst.why: Order from the premise the rest depends on. The three warring projects need consolidating and the documentation is inadequate - but a mapped control set is mapped against obligations, and a card's required contents depend on the tier. Both are being designed against a reading of the law that is wrong in scope, wrong about fraud detection, and silent on a chatbot duty that already applies.

cases.title: The campaign with the cloned voice
cases.brief: A consumer brand's marketing team generates product images, short video and a cloned voice of its brand ambassador for regional-language ads. dpdp.t: A lender’s agent leaks customer data because identifiers were sent unmasked to a vendor, and the lender then fails to notify the Data Protection Board. Using the Act’s maximum penalties of ₹250 crore for failing to take reasonable security safeguards and ₹200 crore for failing to notify a breach, what is the combined maximum exposure, in ₹ crore?
dpdp.a: ₹250 crore + ₹200 crore = ₹450 crore. Actual penalties are set by the Board based on factors such as gravity, duration and mitigation, but the two failures are separate breaches of duty. Masking and a breach runbook remove both.
iv: What does the DPDP Act change for an AI agent that handles customer data?

Every place personal data flows becomes a compliance surface: prompts, retrieved context, agent memory, logs, caches and vendor calls. The agent needs a lawful basis and itemised notice for each purpose, collection limited to that purpose, safeguards such as masking and processor contracts, a breach process that reports without delay and in detail within 72 hours, and erasure that reaches every copy.
When do the DPDP obligations apply?

The Rules were notified on 13 November 2025. The Data Protection Board provisions applied at once, consent managers follow after 12 months, and most substantive obligations, including notice, safeguards, breach reporting and erasure, apply from 13 May 2027. Systems designed now should meet them at launch.
mis: Erasing only from the primary database
Fan erasure out to vector stores, memory, caches and logs
Raw identifiers in prompts and logs
Mask or tokenise before the model and the log see them

finreg.t: A broker has 20 internal AI tools, 3 customer-facing agents and 2 agents that make decisions about customers. If the controls required per system are 3 for internal, 7 for customer-facing and 8 for decision tiers, how many control instances must it evidence?
finreg.a: 20 × 3 + 3 × 7 + 2 × 8 = 60 + 21 + 16 = 97. Tiering matters: treating all 25 as decision-tier would mean 200, and treating all as internal would leave the customer-facing agents short of kill switches, disclosure and review.
iv: What does SEBI Regulation 16C mean for a broker using a vendor’s LLM?

It makes the regulated entity solely responsible for the privacy and security of investor data, for the output of the AI tools it relies on, and for compliance with law, whether the tool is built in-house or bought. Vendor assurances do not transfer that responsibility, so the broker must validate the model, control the data it receives and keep audit rights in the contract.
What does RBI’s FREE-AI framework ask of a bank deploying an agent?

It sets seven principles, or sutras, and recommendations under six pillars. For a deployment that means a board-approved AI policy, an inventory of AI uses by risk, independent testing and audit, telling customers when AI is involved and giving them a way to contest outcomes, incident reporting, and accountability that does not shrink as the system becomes more autonomous.
mis: One set of controls for every AI use
Tier by customer impact and scale the controls
Waiting for final guidelines
Build inventory, validation, kill switches and disclosure now

euai.t: A high-risk provider breaches its obligations. The maximum fine is €15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. With a turnover of €800 million, what is the maximum fine, in € million?
euai.a: 3% of €800 million is €24 million, which is higher than €15 million, so the maximum is €24 million. For prohibited practices the ceiling rises to €35 million or 7%, which would be €56 million here.
iv: Does the EU AI Act apply to an Indian company?

It can. It applies to providers placing AI systems on the EU market and to providers and deployers outside the EU when the system’s output is used in the EU. An Indian fintech scoring the creditworthiness of EU residents, or a broker serving EU clients through a chatbot, is in scope for those systems.
What changed with the Digital Omnibus?

Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force from 27 July 2026, moved the high-risk obligations for Annex III systems such as credit scoring to 2 December 2027 and for product-embedded systems to 2 August 2028. Prohibitions have applied since February 2025, and chatbot transparency duties still apply from 2 August 2026.
mis: Assuming the Act stops at EU borders
Check whether outputs affect EU residents
Ignoring provider versus deployer
Your duties depend on your role for each system

frameworks.t: A bank replaced four separate compliance checklists with one control library, cutting auditor evidence requests from 400 items to 150. By what percentage did the evidence requests fall?
frameworks.a: (400 − 150) ÷ 400 = 62.5%. The saving comes from mapping each control, such as one eval report or one incident runbook, to every framework it satisfies, so it is produced once and cited many times.
iv: How do the NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 differ?

The NIST AI RMF is a voluntary framework organised into Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, with profiles such as the Generative AI Profile; it guides what to do but is not certifiable. ISO/IEC 42001 is a management-system standard with requirements and Annex A controls that an accredited body can certify, which clients often ask for. Many organisations use NIST for risk practice and ISO 42001 for the certifiable system.
Why use a framework if no Indian law requires it?

Because regulators ask for evidence of governance, not for a particular framework. A framework gives a repeatable structure, avoids a separate project per regulation, and lets one well-built control satisfy RBI, SEBI, DPDP and EU expectations at once.
mis: A separate project for each regulation
One control library mapped to all of them
Certificates without working controls
Back every control with evals, red teaming and monitoring

audit.t: A broker’s KYC agent makes 3 million decisions a year. Each hash-chained decision record is 4 KB, and records are kept for 5 years. How much storage do the retained records need, in GB? (Use 1 GB = 1,000,000 KB.)
audit.a: 3,000,000 × 4 KB = 12 GB a year; over 5 years, 60 GB. That is small compared with the cost of being unable to explain one disputed decision; the design constraint is completeness and tamper evidence, not storage.
iv: What should an audit record for an AI decision contain?

Enough to replay the decision: a hash of the input and the extracted fields with personal data masked, the model and prompt versions, the documents and policy clauses used, tool calls and results, the decision and reason codes, the human reviewer and any override with its reason, and timestamps. Records should be append-only and tamper-evident.
How do you make LLM decisions explainable to a regulator?

Constrain the agent to produce structured reason codes tied to written policy clauses, log the evidence each code rests on, and keep a replayable trace with versions. For scored models, feature attributions such as SHAP can support the reason codes. A post-hoc narrative written by the model alone is not an explanation.
mis: Logging only the outcome
Log inputs, versions, grounds, actions and people
Mutable logs
Append-only storage with hash chaining or write-once retention

cards.t: A KYC agent is 94% accurate overall. Scanned regional-language documents are 10% of volume and score 71%. What is the accuracy on the other 90% of documents, in percent?
cards.a: 0.94 = 0.10 × 0.71 + 0.90 × x, so x = (0.94 − 0.071) ÷ 0.90 ≈ 96.6%. The average looks healthy because the weak segment is small, which is exactly why a system card must report results by segment.
iv: What is the difference between a model card and a system card?

A model card documents one model: intended use, training data, evaluation results by subgroup and limitations. A system card documents the whole deployed system around it: the agent’s purpose and out-of-scope uses, the data and legal basis, results by segment, failure modes, human oversight and kill switch, versions and a grievance contact.
How do you keep a system card honest?

Generate it from the same eval results used for release decisions, break results down by the segments customers differ on, state limitations with their mitigations, and version it with the system so every material change produces a new card.
mis: Reporting only the overall average
Show results by language, region and document type
A card written once at launch
Regenerate it with every release

vendor.t: Godavari Bank’s LLM provider offers a 99.9% monthly availability SLA. In a 30-day month, how many minutes of downtime can the provider have without breaching it?
vendor.a: 30 × 24 × 60 = 43,200 minutes. 0.1% of 43,200 = 43.2 minutes. An SLA usually pays service credits, not the bank’s losses, so 43 minutes of complaint handling can stop within the SLA; a tested fallback is what keeps the service up.
iv: How do you run due diligence on an LLM provider for a regulated workload?

Start with the data terms: whether inputs are used for training, how long logs are kept, whether zero data retention is available, where processing happens and which sub-processors are involved. Read the SOC 2 Type II and ISO/IEC 27001 reports, and ISO/IEC 42001 if offered, checking that their scope covers the service you will use. Then put what matters into the contract: SLA, incident notice fast enough for your own reporting clocks, audit and regulator access, sub-processor notice, and data return and deletion on exit.
Why pin model versions, and what does it cost you?

A floating alias lets the provider change the model behind the same name, so behaviour changes in production with no release on your side. Pinning a dated snapshot makes every change a deliberate upgrade that runs through your evals first. The cost is that snapshots retire, so you must track deprecation notices and budget for migrations and eval runs a few times a year.
mis: Treating the vendor as responsible for the vendor’s model
The regulated firm stays accountable; manage the vendor through contract, testing and monitoring
Adding a fallback provider that has never carried traffic
Pin it, give it the same data terms, and drill the failover on a schedule

aiincident.t: A privacy breach is detected at 10:30 on Monday. If a detailed report is due within 72 hours, by what time on which day is it due? Give the number of hours after Monday 00:00.
aiincident.a: 10.5 + 72 = 82.5 hours after Monday 00:00, which is Thursday at 10:30.
iv: How is AI incident management different from IT incident response?

IT response restores service. AI incident management also covers harms that never cause an outage, such as unfair decisions, false or harmful outputs and privacy leaks, and adds a definition, severity scale, register, notification clocks, root cause and verified corrective action, and reporting to the risk committee and regulators.
What would you put in an AI incident playbook?
Harm types and severity criteria, owners, which notifications may apply with deadlines and templates, evidence to capture, and closure criteria. Confirm the rules with legal and compliance.
mis: Counting only outages
Define harms such as unfair outcomes and privacy leaks as incidents
Closing on an unverified fix
Require root cause and a verified corrective action

provenance.t: Visible labels plus metadata survive sharing on 70% of assets. An invisible watermark survives on 85% of the rest. What share stays identifiable overall, in percent?
provenance.a: Missing after labels: 30%. The watermark recovers 85% of those: 0.3 × 0.85 = 25.5%. Total 70 + 25.5 = 95.5%.
iv: How would you mark AI-generated images and audio?

Add a visible label or spoken disclosure by default, sign C2PA Content Credentials, add an invisible watermark tied to an asset id, stop users removing them, and test survival through real sharing paths.
What do India’s 2026 IT Rules amendments require of generative tools?

In summary: intermediaries offering tools that create realistic synthetic audio-visual content must label it prominently, embed permanent metadata or an identifier where feasible, and not allow removal; significant social media intermediaries must also collect user declarations and verify them. Confirm details with counsel.
mis: Relying on metadata alone
Add a watermark; many apps strip metadata
Letting users switch labels off
Lock labels and credentials in the tool

gloss: data fiduciary
Under the DPDP Act, the organisation that decides why and how personal data is processed.
data processor
An entity that processes personal data on a fiduciary’s behalf, such as a model vendor.
data principal
The person the personal data is about; a parent or guardian for a child.
consent manager
A registered entity through which people give, manage and withdraw consent under the DPDP Rules.
Significant Data Fiduciary
A fiduciary designated for volume or risk, with extra duties such as annual impact assessments and audits.
FREE-AI
RBI’s Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of AI (August 2025), with seven sutras and six pillars.
Regulation 16C
SEBI’s 2025 rule making intermediaries solely responsible for data, output and compliance when they use AI tools.
kill switch
A control that stops an AI system’s actions immediately, without a deployment.
AI inventory
A register of every AI use with owner, purpose, model, vendor and risk tier.
high-risk system
An EU AI Act category, such as credit scoring of individuals, with duties on risk management, logs and oversight.
provider and deployer
EU AI Act roles: the provider builds or markets a system; the deployer uses it under its authority.
AI management system
ISO/IEC 42001’s term for the policies, processes and controls that govern AI across an organisation.
hash chain
Records that each include the hash of the previous one, so any edit or deletion is detectable.
reason code
A short, structured statement of why a decision was made, tied to a written rule.
system card
Documentation of a deployed AI system: purpose, data, results by segment, limitations and oversight.
zero data retention
A provider arrangement under which request and response content is not stored after the response is returned, beyond what is needed to serve it.
concentration risk
The risk that many critical services depend on one provider, so a single outage, price change or exit hits all of them at once.
exit plan
A documented, rehearsed plan to move a service off a vendor: what moves, how it is tested, how data is returned and deleted, and how long it takes.
AI incident
An event where an AI system’s development or use causes, or nearly causes, harm to people, property, rights or the environment.
CAPA
Corrective and preventive action: the fix for an incident and the change that stops it recurring.
notification clock
A legal or contractual deadline, counted from detection, for telling a regulator or affected people.
C2PA
An open standard for signed Content Credentials that record how a media file was created and edited.
synthetically generated information
In India’s IT Rules, audio-visual content created or altered by computer to appear real.
invisible watermark
A hidden signal in pixels or audio that marks content as generated and survives many edits.

Next, two bars compare provider changes reaching production each year: 6 silent changes on a floating alias against 0 with a pinned snapshot and evals, and a chip shows a new snapshot scoring 81% against a baseline of 86% being blocked. Finally, an 8-hour provider incident takes a single-provider assistant down for 8 hours, while a tested fallback limits it to 15 minutes, and a badge notes that an exit plan is on file and rehearsed yearly.
